title: York Revolution cancel baseball game after players refuse to wear Pride jerseys
content:
A Pennsylvania independent pro baseball team canceled its Pride Night game Thursday, citing players’ refusal to wear uniforms with rainbow sleeves one week after three San Francisco Giants players altered their own team’s Pride-themed hats.

York Revolution officials said in a statement that the team would forfeit its 11th annual Pride Night game, but the free Pride Night activities would go on as planned.

“Unfortunately, several of our players have refused to wear the scheduled Pride Night jersey and the club decided that hosting the event is more important than forcing players to wear jerseys they are not comfortable with and playing the game,” the statement read.

The team said the players’ reticence to participate “is completely inconsistent with our vision as the Most Welcoming Place in York.” As a gesture of support, officials pledged to donate $10,000 to the Rainbow Rose Center, which organizes events focused on inclusion for the LGBTQIA+ community.

Revolution president and general manager Ben Shipley said fewer than nine players on the 28-man roster were willing to play in the Pride uniforms, leaving the team without enough players to fill its lineup card.

“I’m disappointed that we’re at this point, and I recognize the players’ plight and their unwillingness to cross their line. I also think tolerance is not acceptance,” Shipley told NBC News on Thursday. “I was just asking for tolerance from the team, and they were unwilling to navigate that with me.”

Ticket holders can exchange tickets for a different game as if Thursday’s were rained out.

The player pushback against the Pride-themed event comes on the heels of controversy involving Giants starter Landen Roupp and relievers JT Brubaker and Ryan Walker. The three players altered their Pride-themed uniforms Friday by writing Bible verses on their hats, while reliever Sam Hentges refused to wear his rainbow-themed cap at all, opting for the team’s typical one.

Adding the verses violated MLB rules banning uniform alterations, and the players involved received verbal warnings but were not fined or penalized.

“There is no hate at all. It’s just what I stand for and what I stand in, and I believe in God and that’s me,” Roupp said after the game.

In response to the controversy, Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) sent a letter to MLB commissioner Rob Manfred on Tuesday that framed the situation as part of “a pattern of discrimination” against Christian players.

“MLB has said this is a content-neutral policy and that MLB ‘respect(s) players’ right to free expression,’” Hawley wrote. “But this is dubious, given that MLB is openly promoting a political viewpoint and possibly compelling adherence to that viewpoint.”

MLB declined to comment on Hawley’s letter, but issued its own statement Tuesday.

“To be clear, this routine verbal warning not to wear the hat in future games is not disciplinary and had absolutely nothing to do with the content of the message,” the league said in a statement to The Athletic. “We respect players’ right to free expression. … We have given the same warning numerous times in the past to players for messages such as ‘Dad,’ ‘Happy Mother’s Day, I Love Mom’ and names of family members.”

Conflicts over political messaging in pro sports have also cropped up in recent years in the NHL, NFL and NBA.

In 2023, the NHL banned teams from wearing “specialty” gear on themed nights promoting things like Pride, veteran causes and cancer research. The use of rainbow “Pride tape” on sticks was a particular focal point. The NHL later reversed its Pride tape ban, which it instituted after religious objections from some players.

Nine NFL teams faced criticism earlier this month for not publicly recognizing the start of Pride Month on social media. The teams are the New York Jets, Pittsburgh Steelers, Cleveland Browns, Cincinnati Bengals, Tennessee Titans, Kansas City Chiefs, Las Vegas Raiders, Dallas Cowboys and New Orleans Saints. Some of those franchises abstained last year, as well.

In basketball, the Chicago Bulls waived guard Jaden Ivey for conduct detrimental to the team in March after he posted a social media video that included anti-gay sentiments. Ivey’s former teammates said at the time that the incident was not a one-off and that he had ostracized some of the locker room with his behavior.

The WNBA’s Paige Bueckers, meanwhile, is one of many players in her league who have spoken out in support of Pride awareness. Speaking on the matter after the Dallas Wings’ sold-out Pride Night game last Thursday, Bueckers advocated for open acceptance of others.

“I think it’s really important,” Bueckers said at her postgame news conference. “I feel like this world would be a lot better place if love and inclusivity was just put first. To live in love. To love somebody regardless of who they like, who they love, and just love them for who they are. I think that’s what life is all about.

“I want to live a Christ-like life — to live in love, to live in accepting others, to live a judgment-free life. That’s really what you want to do.”
